title: 1Password customer data, source code taken in GitHub breach
summary: 1Password says customer vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and unaffected as the platform does not have access to user passwords or secret keys

items: 1Password reported a security breach where an attacker accessed an employee's GitHub account, stealing customer data and source code.
The stolen data included user names, email addresses, account identifiers, and public keys, but no sensitive user passwords or secret keys were compromised.
In response, 1Password rotated all exposed credentials, tightened security controls, and advised users to be cautious of phishing attempts related to the incident.

MANILA, Philippines – Password management software 1Password announced on Wednesday, November 25, that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account, stealing some customer data and copying source code from private repositories.
1Password, in its blog post informing the public about the incident, said it began investigations on November 19 following indications someone had taken over an employee’s GitHub account.

It added, however, that customers’ vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected because 1Password does not have access to user passwords or secret keys.
The attacker downloaded account records of a subset of 1Password’s users.

items: Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times
Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)
Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)
Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery
Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

blocks.text: 1Password also said the attacker copied source code from private repositories and gained access to a continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment system (CI/CD). The source code contains no customer data or user secrets, while the CI/CD holds “infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work.”

In light of the attack, 1Password has triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed. It disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.

1Password also said it tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, adding new detections for this kind of attack. It also lengthened invitation codes from six to 10 characters as a precaution.
1Password also validated that no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise was done using any exposed account provisioning tokens.
It also asked help from independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment approaches and remediation efforts.

While 1Password said there was no impact to its services, availability, or product security, it advised users to be wary of “phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.”

The company added, “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.”
It reminded users to keep their secret keys and passwords safe and invited users to report suspicious activity to support@1password.com. – Rappler.com
